name: actor-based
context: Distributed systems requiring high concurrency, fault tolerance, and location transparency where autonomous entities communicate via asynchronous message passing. The actor model treats each actor as the fundamental unit of computation—encapsulating state, behavior, and mailbox—organized in hierarchical supervision trees that enable automatic failure recovery.
benefits: Native concurrency without locks—message passing eliminates race conditions
Fault isolation through supervision hierarchies—failures are contained and recovered automatically
Location transparency—actors operate identically whether local or remote
Elastic scalability—actors distribute across nodes dynamically via clustering and sharding
Backpressure built into mailbox semantics—bounded queues prevent memory exhaustion
Natural fit for event sourcing and event-driven architectures
Self-healing systems via "let it crash" supervision philosophy
tradeoffs: Debugging message flows is complex without proper distributed tracing tools
Async testing requires specialized test harnesses and techniques
Steep learning curve—demands fundamentally different mental model from OOP
Message ordering only guaranteed per-actor, not across actor interactions
Circular message waits can cause deadlocks in poorly designed flows
Per-message overhead makes actor-per-request patterns expensive at scale
Synchronous thinking defeats the async benefits
use_cases: Chat or collaboration platforms with thousands of concurrent sessions
Order processing systems with independent stateful handlers
IoT device gateways managing millions of connections
Multi-agent AI orchestrations with autonomous workers
Fault-tolerant distributed caches with automatic recovery
Event-sourced domains where state transitions are immutable events
avoid_when: Sub-millisecond latency requirements where mailbox queuing adds unpredictable delay
Stateless services that don't benefit from encapsulated state
Small teams with simple requirements that don't justify paradigm shift
CPU-intensive workloads where scheduling overhead hurts throughput
Environments where debugging async message flows is prohibitively difficult
component_types: ActorSystem: Container managing actor lifecycle, dispatching, and mailbox coordination
Actor: Primitive computation unit with private state, behavior, and mailbox
Mailbox: Queue of incoming messages per actor; processes messages sequentially one at a time
Dispatcher: Thread pool that drives actor execution and scheduling
Supervisor: Parent actor implementing restart/resume/stop/escalate strategies
Router: Partitions messages across actor instances for load distribution
ShardCoordinator: Manages actor sharding across cluster nodes
EventSourcedActor: Actor with persisted state via journal replay
anti_patterns: Blocking operations inside actors (starves other actors)
Physical addresses in messages (breaks location transparency)
Shared mutable state between actors (reintroduces race conditions)
Deeply nested hierarchies without timeout boundaries
Ignoring backpressure signals until mailbox overflows
design_principles: Single Responsibility: Each actor performs one well-defined task or domain function
Statelessness: Prefer stateless actors; if state is required, externalize it to persistence
Location Transparency: Actors operate identically whether local or remote; never encode physical addresses
Non-Blocking Handlers: Handlers should not block on I/O; use async APIs and futures
Supervision Hierarchy: Parents supervise children; failures bubble up until handled at appropriate level
Bounded Mailboxes: Use backpressure to prevent memory exhaustion; monitor mailbox depths
Idempotency: Design message handlers to be safe for retry on failure recovery
Error Kernel Pattern: Place critical state high in hierarchy; dangerous operations deep in hierarchy
best_practices: Keep Actors Small: Treat actors like lightweight processes with clear, focused protocols
Use Bounded Queues: Configure mailbox capacities to enable backpressure and prevent memory exhaustion
Make Handlers Non-Blocking: Offload I/O to async APIs; avoid synchronous waits that starve other actors
Model Failures via Supervision: Use restart, resume, stop, escalate strategies appropriately
Prefer Sharding for Distribution: Use partitioning keys that avoid hotspots in actor state
Persist State with Event Sourcing: For durability requirements, journal state transitions; ensure idempotency on replay
Embrace Location Transparency: Never encode physical addresses in message protocols
Instrument with Metrics: Track per-actor metrics—mailbox depth, processing latency, restart counts
Build Hierarchies Explicitly: Structure actors by responsibilities and dependencies
Use OneForOne by Default: Only use AllForOne for tightly coupled actor ensembles
